title: FizzBuzz Functions
story: FizzBuzz is the most famous coding challenge in the world — used in thousands of job interviews to test if someone can think logically with functions. The rules are simple, but the if/elif ordering is a trap that catches the unwary. You're about to master it.
why: FizzBuzz teaches the critical lesson that condition order matters: checking the combined case (FizzBuzz) before the individual cases (Fizz, Buzz) is the difference between correct and broken logic.
analogy: FizzBuzz condition ordering is like airport security lines. The 'FizzBuzz' check (both 3 AND 5) is the VIP lane — it must be checked first. If you put the 'Fizz' lane (divisible by 3) before the VIP lane, VIPs get processed as regular passengers and never reach their intended destination. Always check the most specific (combined) case before the more general (single) cases.

try_it: Extend fizzbuzz to 30 and add a third rule: if divisible by 7, append "Pop". So 21 (divisible by 3 and 7) returns "FizzPop". Think carefully about where to place the new conditions — triple cases come before doubles come before singles.
tips: The most specific condition (both 3 AND 5) goes FIRST — always
Use `and` to combine conditions: `n % 3 == 0 and n % 5 == 0`
Each condition returns immediately — only one branch executes per call
The else clause catches all numbers that don't match any special rule
common_mistakes: Putting `n % 3 == 0` before the combined `n % 3 == 0 and n % 5 == 0` — 15 returns 'Fizz' instead of 'FizzBuzz'
Using `or` instead of `and` for the combined case — any number divisible by 3 OR 5 would match
Forgetting the else clause — numbers that aren't divisible by 3 or 5 must still return something
Writing separate if statements instead of if/elif — multiple branches could execute for the same number
